# Clinical Vignette: Amara

Amara is a twenty-year-old pharmacist who relocated to the United States three years ago to pursue her degree. She comes from a West African country where her family still resides, and she speaks with quiet deliberation, choosing her words carefully. She is engaged to a man she has known since childhood, and they maintain their relationship across the distance through video calls and messages. To those who know her professionally at the pharmacy where she works part-time, she appears competent and reliable—the kind of colleague who arrives early and stays focused on her tasks.

Six years ago, when Amara was fourteen, her country experienced civil unrest that escalated into violence in her region. She was detained by armed militia for five days along with other young people they had rounded up from her neighborhood. During her captivity, she endured repeated beatings, sleep deprivation, and threats of worse harm. The soldiers would wake her throughout the night, forcing her to stand for hours or kneel on concrete. They used interrogation tactics meant to terrify—pointing weapons at her head, threatening her family, subjecting her to psychological manipulation designed to break her will. She was released after her father paid a ransom, but the experience left invisible scars that would resurface years later.

For a long time after her release, Amara seemed to recover. She returned to school, performed well academically, and eventually earned her place in a pharmacy program abroad. In many ways, she had escaped. But escape, she has come to understand, is not the same as healing.

The symptoms began subtly during her first year of university. Loud noises—a car backfiring, someone slamming a door—would send her heart racing. She would find herself unable to breathe, her body flooded with the certainty that danger was imminent. She started avoiding certain places on campus, taking longer routes to classes to avoid crowds. She stopped going to social events. Her fiancé noticed she would sometimes become distant during their calls, staring past the camera with an expression he couldn't reach.

The pharmacist work triggered something deeper. Handling medications, managing inventory, following protocols—the structure should have felt safe. Instead, the rigid routines and enclosed space of the pharmacy sometimes felt suffocating. When customers would raise their voices in frustration about insurance or wait times, Amara would freeze, her mind suddenly transporting her back to the militia compound. She has had moments where she cannot remember what medication she was retrieving, her mind simply blank, as though she has temporarily left her own body.

At night, sleep eludes her. When it comes, nightmares arrive with it—fragmented images of detention, of hands grabbing her, of voices shouting commands in languages she doesn't understand. She wakes gasping, her sheets soaked with sweat, and spends hours unable to return to sleep. During the day, she feels perpetually tired, moving through her shifts as though underwater.

She has begun to isolate further, declining her fiancé's suggestions that she visit home or that he visit her. She worries that if she goes back, the memories will overwhelm her completely. She worries that if he sees her like this—fractured and afraid—he will realize she is not the girl he once knew. Lately, she has found herself questioning whether she deserves to have a normal life, whether the trauma that happened to her is somehow a permanent part of her identity that cannot be separated from who she is meant to become.
